title: NumPy
body:
The lab toolchain for this course: two hours a week running the syllabus on real datasets, in
Python with **NumPy** and **SciPy**, or in MATLAB. It is the only math course in the degree with
an implementation component, and it is the reason the course profile puts algorithms on real data
ahead of theory.

NumPy's `ndarray` is a dense typed [[Array]] with a shape, so a [[Matrix]] is a 2D one and a
[[Vector]] a 1D one. The operations map straight onto the notes:

| Call | Note |
|---|---|
| `A @ B` | [[Matrix Multiplication]] |
| `np.linalg.svd(A)` | [[Singular Value Decomposition]] |
| `np.linalg.eigh(A)` | [[Spectral Theorem]], the symmetric case |
| `np.linalg.qr(A)` | [[Gram-Schmidt]], done by Householder reflections |
| `np.linalg.lstsq(A, b)` | [[Least Squares]] |
| `np.linalg.pinv(A)` | [[Pseudoinverse]] |
| `np.linalg.norm(v, ord=1)` | [[Vector Norm]] |
| `sklearn.decomposition.PCA` | [[Principal Component Analysis]], a truncated SVD underneath |

Two habits the lab teaches that the theory does not. **Never call `inv`**: use `solve`, `lstsq`,
or `pinv`, for the conditioning reasons [[Matrix Inverse]] and [[Least Squares]] both give.
And **vectorise**: a Python loop over a million elements is slow because it is a million
interpreted iterations, while the same work as an array expression is one call into compiled
BLAS. Same $O(n^3)$ [[Time Complexity]] for a matrix product either way, and a constant factor of
a hundred between them, which is the cleanest demonstration in the degree that asymptotics are not
the whole story.

This is also the vault's only real connection to [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE]],
the Python course.
